issues.legal_issue: Dropping the original lessors from the proceedings does not defeat a claim to enforce an agreement made with other contracting parties when the agreement recognizes that those parties had acquired the relevant rights.
material_facts: The agreement sought to be enforced was made with the developer and its director, not with the original lessors.
The agreement recited the transfer of the original lessors’ rights to the contracting parties and recorded the purchaser’s acceptance of the title derived through them.
A later assignment of the building and associated land interests also recited that the original lessors had surrendered their rights to the developer.
issues.conclusion: The objection that the claim must fail because the original lessors were no longer parties to the proceedings was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A claim to enforce an agreement may proceed against its contracting parties where the agreement and the undisputed record show that the relevant rights had passed from the original holders to those parties; dropping the original holders does not by itself defeat enforcement.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.agreement_with_remaining_defendants: The parties remaining in the proceeding are the parties who made the agreement sought to be enforced.
predicates.agreement_recites_transfer_from_original: The agreement records that the relevant rights passed from the original rights holders to the contracting parties.

issues.definition: When a property-sale enforcement proceeding is against the contracting parties and their agreement records the transfer of the relevant rights to them from the original rights holders, dropping those original holders does not defeat enforcement.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell property is not rendered unenforceable merely because performance requires permissions or other action by public authorities, unless the required permission has been finally refused so as to make performance impossible.
material_facts: The agreement concerned a flat in a building that remained incomplete after construction stopped following a dispute over the lease and building permissions.
The purchaser was found to have remained ready and willing to perform her contractual obligations and offered to accept the flat in its existing condition.
The required lease renewal and building-plan revalidation had not been finally refused.
The developer had assigned the rest of the building and the associated land interests to another purchaser despite the asserted obstacles.
The Court considered that performance could be made conditional on the authorities granting the necessary approvals.
issues.conclusion: The Court granted conditional specific performance, with execution of the conveyance dependent on the necessary lease renewal and plan revalidation; if the authorities refused them and performance thereby became impossible, the decree could not be executed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10 and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, including the presumption in Explanation (i) to Section 10, specific performance of an agreement concerning immovable property is not refused merely because the vendor must obtain official permission. The vendor has an implied obligation to take necessary steps to obtain it. Unless the competent authority has finally rejected the required permission and the rejection makes performance impossible, a court may order conditional specific performance. This approach follows Rojasara Ramjibhai Dahyabhai v. Jani Narottamdas Lallubhai, Mrs. Chandnee Widyavati Madden v. Dr. C.L. Katial, and Ramesh Chandra Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal. The Court also applied the discretionary principles in Section 20 described in Sardar Singh v. Krishna Devi and K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd.; it distinguished cases where performance had become impossible or the contract had been frustrated under Section 56 of the Contract Act.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and immovable_property_agreement and required_public_approvals_pending and approvals_not_finally_refused and purchaser_ready_and_willing

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.immovable_property_agreement: The agreement concerns immovable property that exists or is to be constructed to agreed specifications.
predicates.required_public_approvals_pending: Performance requires permissions or other action from public authorities that have not yet been obtained.
predicates.approvals_not_finally_refused: The competent authorities have not finally refused the required permissions in a way that makes performance impossible.
predicates.purchaser_ready_and_willing: The purchaser has remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns specific performance of a property-sale agreement, necessary public approvals remain pending but have not been finally refused, and the purchaser is ready and willing, the court may condition specific performance on obtaining those approvals.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be made subject to additional compensation and proportionate sharing of related expenses where delay, substantial property-value appreciation, incomplete performance, and the parties’ respective responsibilities make unconditional enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The purchaser had paid only part of the agreed consideration and had not paid the balance after construction stopped.
The property had substantially increased in value over the long period of delay.
The delay and obstacles were not attributable solely to the developer; other parties, public authorities, and related proceedings also affected performance.
The purchaser was willing to take the incomplete flat and contribute a share of expenses associated with obtaining the necessary approvals.
The Court found that granting the purchaser the full benefit of the increased value without an adjustment would be inequitable.
issues.conclusion: The Court conditioned specific performance on an additional compensatory payment to the sellers, as well as the purchaser’s contribution to her proportionate share of expenses and monetary commitments associated with obtaining the necessary approvals. If she did not satisfy the payment condition, specific performance would be denied and the remedies under the earlier decree would remain available.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary and requires the court to exercise that discretion on sound judicial principles after considering the circumstances, conduct of the parties, hardship, and comparative equities. Mere price escalation does not automatically bar or compel specific performance, but it may be considered in balancing equities. The Court relied on Sardar Singh v. Krishna Devi, K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd., K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal, and Gobind Ram v. Gian Chand. It also applied the principle that compensation may be used to balance equities while granting specific performance, as discussed in Gobind Ram, and considered the principles in Her Highness Maharani Shantidevi P. Gaikwad v. Savjibhai Haribhai Patel.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and purchaser_ready_and_willing and substantial_property_value_increase and only_part_of_price_paid and delay_not_solely_attributable_to_seller and performance_requires_shared_expenses

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a refusal to grant specific performance.
predicates.purchaser_ready_and_willing: The purchaser has been found ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.
predicates.substantial_property_value_increase: The property has substantially increased in value during the delay in performance.
predicates.only_part_of_price_paid: The purchaser has paid only part of the agreed price and has not paid the balance.
predicates.delay_not_solely_attributable_to_seller: Other parties, public authorities, or related proceedings also contributed to the delay or obstacles to performance.
predicates.performance_requires_shared_expenses: Completing performance requires expenses or monetary commitments that the purchaser must share proportionately.

issues.definition: When a ready and willing purchaser seeks specific performance after substantial property-value appreciation, has paid only part of the price, did not face delay caused solely by the seller, and must share expenses needed for performance, specific performance may be conditioned on compensatory payment and proportionate expense sharing.
